claim: The first S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) degrading enzyme (SAMase) was discovered in bacteriophage T3.
source: The first S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) degrading enzyme (SAMase) was discovered in bacteriophage T3, as a counter-defense against the bacterial restriction-modification system, and annotated as a SAM hydrolase forming 5'-methyl-thioadenosine (MTA) and L-homoserine.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to historical literature in the introduction.

claim: T3 SAMase was annotated as a SAM hydrolase forming 5'-methyl-thioadenosine (MTA) and L-homoserine.
source: The first S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) degrading enzyme (SAMase) was discovered in bacteriophage T3, as a counter-defense against the bacterial restriction-modification system, and annotated as a SAM hydrolase forming 5'-methyl-thioadenosine (MTA) and L-homoserine.
evidence: This historical annotation is stated in the abstract and discussed in the introduction with citations to Gold and Hurwitz, 1964 and Hausmann, 1967.

claim: Three SAMases from environmental phages have barely detectable sequence similarity to T3 SAMase.
source: From environmental phages, we recently discovered three SAMases with barely detectable sequence similarity to T3 SAMase and without homology to proteins of known structure.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The newly discovered SAMases have no homology to proteins of known structure.
source: From environmental phages, we recently discovered three SAMases with barely detectable sequence similarity to T3 SAMase and without homology to proteins of known structure.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by the fact that this is the first structure determination of this enzyme family.

claim: Svi3-3 structure shows a trimer of alpha–beta sandwiches similar to the GlnB-like superfamily.
source: The structure shows a trimer of alpha–beta sandwiches similar to the GlnB-like superfamily, with active sites formed at the trimer interfaces.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 2A and B, with structural comparison discussed in the Results section.

claim: Active sites are formed at the trimer interfaces in Svi3-3.
source: The structure shows a trimer of alpha–beta sandwiches similar to the GlnB-like superfamily, with active sites formed at the trimer interfaces.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 2C showing SAH binding at the interface between two subunits.

claim: Phage-encoded SAMases are lyases, not hydrolases, forming MTA and L-homoserine lactone.
source: Quantum-mechanical calculations, thin-layer chromatography, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy demonstrate that this family of enzymes are not hydrolases but lyases forming MTA and L-homoserine lactone in a unimolecular reaction mechanism.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract and supported by DFT calculations (Figure 7), TLC (Figure 9A), and NMR (Figure 9B).

claim: The SAMase reaction proceeds through a unimolecular reaction mechanism.
source: Quantum-mechanical calculations, thin-layer chromatography, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy demonstrate that this family of enzymes are not hydrolases but lyases forming MTA and L-homoserine lactone in a unimolecular reaction mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by DFT calculations showing intramolecular carboxylate oxygen attack (Figure 7).

claim: T3 SAMase belongs to the same structural family as Svi3-3.
source: Sequence analysis and in vitro and in vivo mutagenesis support that T3 SAMase belongs to the same structural family and utilizes the same reaction mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structure-guided sequence alignment (Figure 5) and mutagenesis data (Table 2).

claim: T3 SAMase utilizes the same reaction mechanism as Svi3-3.
source: Sequence analysis and in vitro and in vivo mutagenesis support that T3 SAMase belongs to the same structural family and utilizes the same reaction mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mutagenesis of conserved residues (Table 2) and TLC showing homoserine lactone formation (Figure 9A).

claim: SAM is an essential methyl donor for methyltransferases that act on nucleic acids, proteins, lipids, and small molecules.
source: It is an essential methyl donor for methyltransferases that act on nucleic acids, proteins, lipids, and small molecules, but is also involved in many other reactions, for example, as a substrate used in biosynthesis of polyamines and quorum sensing molecules (reviewed in Loenen, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to a review by Loenen, 2006.

claim: SAM is involved in biosynthesis of polyamines and quorum sensing molecules.
source: It is an essential methyl donor for methyltransferases that act on nucleic acids, proteins, lipids, and small molecules, but is also involved in many other reactions, for example, as a substrate used in biosynthesis of polyamines and quorum sensing molecules (reviewed in Loenen, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Loenen, 2006.

claim: SAM is involved in epigenetic changes in many organisms.
source: It is also involved in epigenetic changes in many organisms (Janke et al., 2015; Su et al., 2016) and in bacterial restriction-modification systems where methylation of DNA is used to distinguish foreign DNA from host DNA (Wilson and Murray, 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Janke et al., 2015 and Su et al., 2016.

claim: In bacterial restriction-modification systems, methylation of DNA is used to distinguish foreign DNA from host DNA.
source: It is also involved in epigenetic changes in many organisms (Janke et al., 2015; Su et al., 2016) and in bacterial restriction-modification systems where methylation of DNA is used to distinguish foreign DNA from host DNA (Wilson and Murray, 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Wilson and Murray, 1991.

claim: Infection of E. coli with phage T3 reduced the degree of methylation of DNA, tRNA, and rRNA.
source: In early studies of nucleic acid methylation, it was observed that while infection of Escherichia coli with phage T1, T2, and T4 induced higher levels of DNA methylation, infection with phage T3 reduced the degree of methylation of not only DNA, but also tRNA and rRNA (Gold and Hurwitz, 1964).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Gold and Hurwitz, 1964.

claim: T3 infection was associated with an immediate and dramatic lowering of SAM levels in E. coli cell extract.
source: The reduction of methylation by T3 infection was associated with an immediate and dramatic lowering of the level of SAM in the E. coli cell extract.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction, referring to observations by Gold and Hurwitz, 1964.

claim: The degradation products of SAM by T3 were identified as MTA and L-homoserine using paper chromatography and chemical tests.
source: The degradation products were, using paper chromatography and chemical tests, identified as 5'-methyl-thioadenosine (MTA) and L-homoserine (Gold and Hurwitz, 1964; Figure 1, top), which led to the claimed discovery of a potent T3-encoded SAM hydrolase enzyme (Hausmann, 1967).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Gold and Hurwitz, 1964 and Hausmann, 1967.

claim: T3 SAMase was produced early in infection.
source: Subsequent work showed that the T3 SAMase was produced early in infection (Gefter et al., 1966), encoded in the early transcribed portion of the phage genome (Herrlich and Schweiger, 1970) and important for the counter defense of the bacteriophage against the type I restriction modification (RM) system of the host bacterium.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Gefter et al., 1966.

claim: T3 SAMase is encoded in the early transcribed portion of the phage genome.
source: Subsequent work showed that the T3 SAMase was produced early in infection (Gefter et al., 1966), encoded in the early transcribed portion of the phage genome (Herrlich and Schweiger, 1970) and important for the counter defense of the bacteriophage against the type I restriction modification (RM) system of the host bacterium.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Herrlich and Schweiger, 1970.

claim: T3 SAMase is important for counter defense against the type I restriction modification system.
source: Subsequent work showed that the T3 SAMase was produced early in infection (Gefter et al., 1966), encoded in the early transcribed portion of the phage genome (Herrlich and Schweiger, 1970) and important for the counter defense of the bacteriophage against the type I restriction modification (RM) system of the host bacterium.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to work on anti-restriction activity.

claim: Lowered SAM levels prevented methylation of the host genome and SAM-dependent restriction of the phage genome.
source: First, the lowered SAM levels prevented methylation of the host genome and the SAM-dependent restriction of the phage genome (Krueger et al., 1975).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as one mechanism for RM system impairment, with citation to Krueger et al., 1975.

claim: Inhibition of restriction was observed to be independent of SAM degradation and possibly linked to an interaction with the restriction enzyme.
source: Second, inhibition was observed to be independent of SAM degradation and possibly linked to an interaction with the restriction enzyme (Spoerel et al., 1979; Studier and Movva, 1976).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Spoerel et al., 1979 and Studier and Movva, 1976.

claim: Three additional SAM degrading enzymes were identified in a screen for bacteriophage DNA that could rescue an ilvA deletion mutant.
source: Recently, three additional SAM degrading enzymes were identified in a screen for bacteriophage DNA that could rescue an auxotrophic E. coli mutant where the isoleucine biosynthetic ilvA gene was deleted.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to work by Jerlström Hultqvist et al., 2018.

claim: Phage-encoded polypeptides induced up-regulation of the methionine biosynthetic pathway by degradation of SAM.
source: Investigations using proteomics and RNA-seq showed that the phage-encoded polypeptides induced up-regulation of the biosynthetic pathway for methionine by degradation of SAM (Jerlström Hultqvist et al., 2018), which together with the repressor protein MetJ acts as a co-repressor of the met regulon (Weissbach and Brot, 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Jerlström Hultqvist et al., 2018 and Weissbach and Brot, 1991.

claim: SAM together with MetJ acts as a co-repressor of the met regulon.
source: Investigations using proteomics and RNA-seq showed that the phage-encoded polypeptides induced up-regulation of the biosynthetic pathway for methionine by degradation of SAM (Jerlström Hultqvist et al., 2018), which together with the repressor protein MetJ acts as a co-repressor of the met regulon (Weissbach and Brot, 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Weissbach and Brot, 1991.

claim: Isoleucine biosynthesis was rescued through a promiscuous activity of MetB.
source: Isoleucine biosynthesis was rescued through a promiscuous activity of one of the up-regulated enzymes, MetB (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Svi3-3 catalyzed conversion of SAM to MTA in vitro.
source: In vitro activity assays demonstrated that Svi3-3 catalyzed conversion of SAM to MTA.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction referring to previous work by Jerlström Hultqvist et al., 2018.

claim: Svi3-3_d19 crystals diffracted to 1.45 Å resolution in space group F4132.
source: The crystals diffracted to 1.45 Å resolution in space group F4132 and the structure was solved using ab initio methods with Arcimboldo (Rodríguez et al., 2009; Figure 2A,F, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 1.

claim: The Svi3-3 structure was solved using ab initio methods with Arcimboldo.
source: The crystals diffracted to 1.45 Å resolution in space group F4132 and the structure was solved using ab initio methods with Arcimboldo (Rodríguez et al., 2009; Figure 2A,F, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Rodríguez et al., 2009.

claim: There is one monomer in the asymmetric unit of Svi3-3 crystals, forming a trimer around the threefold crystallographic axis.
source: There is one monomer in the asymmetric unit, forming a trimer around the threefold crystallographic axis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the crystal structure.

claim: The C-terminal 16 residues of Svi3-3 are disordered.
source: Apart from the disordered C-terminal 16 residues, the full structure could be built.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the structure determination.

claim: Svi3-3 forms a trimer of ferredoxin-like fold alpha–beta sandwiches.
source: Svi3-3 forms a trimer of ferredoxin-like fold alpha–beta sandwiches, where each subunit has two helices on the outside and a five-stranded anti-parallel beta sheet at the center (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Each Svi3-3 subunit has two helices on the outside and a five-stranded anti-parallel beta sheet at the center.
source: Svi3-3 forms a trimer of ferredoxin-like fold alpha–beta sandwiches, where each subunit has two helices on the outside and a five-stranded anti-parallel beta sheet at the center (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Svi3-3 subunits are in a 'velcro-like' topology where residues 2–6 at the N terminus of one subunit form beta-sheet interactions with residues 120–124 in β8 of another subunit.
source: The subunits pack in a triangular manner, forming continuous beta sheets with their neighbors and are each in a 'velcro-like' topology where residues 2–6 at the N terminus of one subunit form beta-sheet interactions with residues 120–124 in β8 of another subunit (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The trimer interfaces are each stabilized by a single salt bridge, numerous hydrogen bonds, and hydrophobic interactions at the center.
source: The trimer interfaces are each stabilized by a single salt bridge, numerous hydrogen bonds, and by hydrophobic interactions at the center.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the trimer structure.

claim: SAH binds at the interface between two subunits in Svi3-3.
source: The substrate analogue SAH binds at the interface between two subunits (Figure 2C and D), enclosed by the β5–β6 hairpin at the edge of the sheet.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The adenosine base of SAH is recognized by interactions with the backbone carbonyl and amide of Ile77 and the side chain of Ser50.
source: The adenosine base is recognized by interactions with the backbone carbonyl and amide of Ile77 and the side chain of Ser50.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing SAH binding.

claim: The ribose of SAH forms interactions with Ser50 from one subunit and Glu69 and Ser71 from another subunit.
source: The ribose forms interactions with Ser50 from one subunit and Glu69 and Ser71 from the other subunit.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing SAH binding.

claim: The homoserine moiety of SAH forms interactions with backbone groups and the side chains of Glu69 and Gln104.
source: The homoserine moiety forms interactions with backbone groups and the side chains of Glu69 and Gln104.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing SAH binding.

claim: In the structure from co-crystallization with SAM, catalysis has occurred and the product MTA is observed.
source: In the structure from co-crystallization with SAM, catalysis has occurred and the product MTA is observed in identical position as the corresponding part of SAH, with the methyl group pointing away from Glu69 (Figure 2E and F), while a proline molecule from the cryo buffer is bound in the second half of the active site, mimicking the second product.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: A proline molecule from the cryo buffer is bound in the active site, mimicking the second product.
source: In the structure from co-crystallization with SAM, catalysis has occurred and the product MTA is observed in identical position as the corresponding part of SAH, with the methyl group pointing away from Glu69 (Figure 2E and F), while a proline molecule from the cryo buffer is bound in the second half of the active site, mimicking the second product.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The protein structures are virtually identical in the presence of SAH and MTA (RMSD of 0.16 Å over 129 Cα atoms).
source: The protein structures are virtually identical in the presence of SAH and MTA (root mean square deviation [RMSD] of 0.16 Å over 129 Cα atoms).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing the two structures.

claim: The N-terminally truncated construct lacking the disordered C terminus provided similar rescue to full-length Svi3-3 in vivo.
source: Indeed, the N-terminally truncated construct additionally lacking the disordered C terminus provided similar rescue to full-length Svi3-3, indicating that neither tail is needed for SAMase activity (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing in vivo complementation assays.

claim: The structure of Svi3-3 in apo state is overall very similar to the complex structures (RMSD of 0.84 Å over 124 Cα atoms).
source: The structure of Svi3-3 in apo state is overall very similar to the complex structures (RMSD of 0.84 Å over 124 Cα atoms), but there is a shift of the N terminus, a conformational change of residues 7–9 to form a more extensive interaction with β9 and the preceding loop of the neighboring subunit, leading to a slight loosening of the trimer (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the apo structure, residues 64 and 65 in the β5–β6 hairpin are disordered.
source: In addition, residues 64 and 65 in the β5–β6 hairpin are disordered.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the apo structure.

claim: SAXS data confirmed that Svi3-3 has a similar trimeric structure in apo state as in the presence of SAM.
source: Small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) data confirmed that Svi3-3 has a similar trimeric structure in apo state as in the presence of SAM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that product release and substrate binding do not require trimer dissociation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Product release and substrate binding do not require trimer dissociation in Svi3-3.
source: Small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) data confirmed that Svi3-3 has a similar trimeric structure in apo state as in the presence of SAM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that product release and substrate binding do not require trimer dissociation.
evidence: This is inferred from SAXS data showing similar trimeric structures in apo and SAM-bound states.

claim: Bacterial PII signaling proteins and CutA-type cation tolerance proteins have similar trimeric architectures to Svi3-3.
source: A search for structures with similar fold and connectivity as Svi3-3 using PDBeFold (Krissinel and Henrick, 2004) showed that bacterial PII signaling proteins and cation tolerance proteins of CutA type (belonging to a PII-like family) in the GlnB-like superfamily have similar trimeric architectures of ferredoxin-like folds.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing structural similarity searches.

claim: The closest structural neighbors to Svi3-3 superpose with RMSDs above 2 Å over no more than 86 Cα atoms.
source: The closest structural neighbors superpose with RMSDs above 2 Å over no more than 86 Cα atoms.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing structural similarity.

claim: PII regulatory proteins bind ATP/ADP and 2-oxoglutarate at the trimer interface.
source: PII regulatory proteins bind ATP/ADP and 2-oxoglutarate at the trimer interface, and conformational changes of loops in response to ligand binding and modification modulates binding to other proteins (Forchhammer and Lüddecke, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Forchhammer and Lüddecke, 2016.

claim: The position of ATP in PII proteins is similar to where SAH binds to Svi3-3.
source: Intriguingly, the position of ATP is similar to where SAH binds to Svi3-3, although the binding site appears non-conserved.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing binding sites.

claim: Glu69 is the most likely catalytic residue in Svi3-3 based on proximity to the site of cleavage.
source: Inspection of the active site shows that Glu69 is relatively close to the site of cleavage (Figure 2C), making this residue the most likely candidate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The Y58F mutant of Svi3-3 eluted mainly as monomer, indicating a de-stabilized trimer.
source: The Y58F mutant eluted mainly as monomer, indicating a de-stabilized trimer, while all other mutants migrated as trimers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing mutant characterization.

claim: Wild-type truncated Svi3-3 showed an average turnover of 9.5 s−1 at 25°C.
source: The WT truncated Svi3-3 construct showed an average turnover of 9.5 s−1 at 25°C, nearly doubled compared to the full length, His-tagged construct (Jerlström Hultqvist et al., 2018), but with significant deviation between batches.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing activity assays.

claim: The Y58F mutant showed fivefold reduced activity compared to wild-type Svi3-3.
source: For the Y58F and E105Q mutants, activity was fivefold and threefold reduced, whereas for the E69Q and E69A mutants, activity was nearly abolished (4500- and 1500-fold reduction).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The E105Q mutant showed threefold reduced activity compared to wild-type Svi3-3.
source: For the Y58F and E105Q mutants, activity was fivefold and threefold reduced, whereas for the E69Q and E69A mutants, activity was nearly abolished (4500- and 1500-fold reduction).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The E69Q mutant showed 4500-fold reduced activity compared to wild-type Svi3-3.
source: For the Y58F and E105Q mutants, activity was fivefold and threefold reduced, whereas for the E69Q and E69A mutants, activity was nearly abolished (4500- and 1500-fold reduction).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The E69A mutant showed 1500-fold reduced activity compared to wild-type Svi3-3.
source: For the Y58F and E105Q mutants, activity was fivefold and threefold reduced, whereas for the E69Q and E69A mutants, activity was nearly abolished (4500- and 1500-fold reduction).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Glu69 is critical for substrate binding, catalysis, or both in vitro.
source: Thus, Glu69 is in vitro critical for substrate binding, catalysis, or both.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the nearly abolished activity of E69Q and E69A mutants.

claim: In the presence of SAM, SAH, or MTA, the melting temperature of wild-type Svi3-3 increased by up to 30°C.
source: In the presence of the substrate SAM, its analogue SAH, or the reaction product MTA, the melting temperature of the WT enzyme increased by up to 30°C, demonstrating a major stabilizing effect on the structure (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The E69Q mutant is not impaired in binding of SAM or MTA.
source: The DSF assay clearly demonstrates that the E69Q mutant is not impaired in binding of SAM or MTA, but that binding of SAH is abolished (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The E69Q mutant does not bind SAH.
source: The DSF assay clearly demonstrates that the E69Q mutant is not impaired in binding of SAM or MTA, but that binding of SAH is abolished (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Only three amino acids are strictly conserved among the aligned SAMases.
source: Only three amino acids are strictly conserved, and only a handful conservatively substituted.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the sequence alignment shown in Figure 5.

claim: All conserved residues in the SAMase alignment are important for binding of SAM.
source: Based on the SAH structure, all the conserved residues are important for binding of SAM.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: Gly56 packs against the ribose in SAM, not allowing space for a side chain.
source: Gly56 packs against the ribose, not allowing space for a side chain, Glu69 and Gln104 as described above form hydrogen bonds to the ligand, and Tyr58 packs against the γ carbon and forms a hydrogen bond to Glu105, enclosing the ligand.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing conserved residues.

claim: Glu69 and Gln104 form hydrogen bonds to SAM.
source: Gly56 packs against the ribose, not allowing space for a side chain, Glu69 and Gln104 as described above form hydrogen bonds to the ligand, and Tyr58 packs against the γ carbon and forms a hydrogen bond to Glu105, enclosing the ligand.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing conserved residues.

claim: Tyr58 packs against the γ carbon of SAM and forms a hydrogen bond to Glu105.
source: Gly56 packs against the ribose, not allowing space for a side chain, Glu69 and Gln104 as described above form hydrogen bonds to the ligand, and Tyr58 packs against the γ carbon and forms a hydrogen bond to Glu105, enclosing the ligand.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing conserved residues.

claim: The T3 SAMase E68Q mutant retained 20–30% activity compared to wild-type.
source: The E68Q mutant of T3 SAMase retained 20–30% activity compared to WT.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing mutagenesis of T3 SAMase.

claim: No rescue was observed for Svi3-3 E69Q, Svi3-3 E69A, Orf1 E50Q, or T3 SAMase E68Q mutants in vivo.
source: No rescue was observed either for the Svi3-3 E69Q, Svi3-3 E69A, Orf1 E50Q, or the T3 SAMase E68Q mutants, suggesting a lost or reduced activity of these variants (Table 2) and validating the sequence alignment.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 2.

claim: Mutations of E67Q in T3 SAMase and D51N in Orf1 still allowed rescue under the same conditions as wild-type.
source: Mutations of the neighboring acidic residues (E67Q in T3 SAMase and D51N in Orf1) still allowed rescue under the same conditions as the corresponding WT.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 2.

claim: For the T3 SAMase E68Q mutant, growth was only observed at the highest concentration of arabinose (0.1%).
source: For the E68Q mutant, growth was only observed at the highest concentration of arabinose (0.1%), where low enzymatic activity can be compensated by increased enzyme levels (Supplementary file 1-table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Supplementary file 1-table 2.

claim: 100 ns of MD simulation was run for both apo Svi3-3 and the SAM complex.
source: A total of 100 ns of MD simulation was run for both apo Svi3-3 and the SAM complex (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing MD simulations.

claim: The SAM conformation in the active site is very stable during MD simulation, particularly the methionine part.
source: The simulation of the complex revealed that the SAM conformation in the active site is very stable, particularly the methionine part (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The carboxylate group of SAM is strongly stabilized by the backbone amide hydrogens of Glu105 and Ser106.
source: In agreement with the experimental structure with SAH, the carboxylate group is strongly stabilized by the backbone amide hydrogens of Glu105 and Ser106, whereas the amino group is primarily stabilized by the side-chains of Glu69 and Gln104 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The amino group of SAM is primarily stabilized by the side-chains of Glu69 and Gln104.
source: In agreement with the experimental structure with SAH, the carboxylate group is strongly stabilized by the backbone amide hydrogens of Glu105 and Ser106, whereas the amino group is primarily stabilized by the side-chains of Glu69 and Gln104 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The positively charged methionine S atom is stabilized through a π-cation interaction with the Tyr58 side-chain.
source: Moreover, the positively charged methionine S atom is consistently stabilized through a π-cation interaction with the Tyr58 side-chain (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Svi3-3 is more flexible in apo state than with SAM in the active site during MD simulation.
source: Comparison of the average root mean square fluctuation (RMSF) of the protein backbone shows that Svi3-3 is more flexible throughout the 100 ns MD simulation in apo state (RMSF for trimer 0.91 Å2) than with SAM in the active site (RMSF for trimer 0.86 Å2) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Residues surrounding the active site become significantly more flexible in apo simulations.
source: Interestingly, the residues surrounding the active site cavity, and in particular the methionine-stabilizing residues 104–106, become significantly more flexible in the apo simulations (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Apo Svi3-3 shows the highest flexibility in the regions surrounding the active site.
source: Thus, 100 ns of MD simulation demonstrated that apo Svi3-3 shows the highest flexibility in the regions surrounding the active site, and that these regions become significantly more rigid upon substrate binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section summarizing MD findings.

claim: Active site regions become significantly more rigid upon substrate binding in Svi3-3.
source: Thus, 100 ns of MD simulation demonstrated that apo Svi3-3 shows the highest flexibility in the regions surrounding the active site, and that these regions become significantly more rigid upon substrate binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section summarizing MD findings.

claim: DFT calculations failed to locate any stationary point for Glu69 attacking the γ-carbon of SAM.
source: DFT geometry optimizations furthermore failed to locate any stationary point (transition state) for the attack, suggesting that the role as a nucleophile is also unlikely.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing DFT calculations.

claim: The main role of Glu69 is to bind and orient the substrate in the active site.
source: Thus, it seems that the main role of Glu69 is to bind and orient the substrate in the active site by accepting H-bonds primarily from the amino group of SAM, but also from the 3'-hydroxyl group of the ribose ring (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on DFT calculations and structural analysis.

claim: DFT calculations could exclude the possibility of Tyr58 acting as a nucleophile in a hydrolase mechanism.
source: However, DFT calculations could exclude the possibility of Tyr58 acting as a nucleophile in such a mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing DFT calculations.

claim: DFT geometry optimization revealed a unimolecular reaction resulting in the formation of homoserine lactone.
source: Further DFT geometry optimization, however, revealed a completely different mechanism, a unimolecular reaction resulting in the formation of homoserine lactone (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The activation energy for the formation of homoserine lactone was calculated to be 16.8 kcal/mol.
source: The activation energy for the formation of homoserine lactone in the DFT cluster model was calculated to be 16.8 kcal/mol with an exothermic reaction energy of −5.7 kcal/mol (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The reaction energy for homoserine lactone formation is −5.7 kcal/mol.
source: The activation energy for the formation of homoserine lactone in the DFT cluster model was calculated to be 16.8 kcal/mol with an exothermic reaction energy of −5.7 kcal/mol (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The calculated barrier for water attacking homoserine lactone is 17.5 kcal/mol.
source: The calculated barrier for this step is 17.5 kcal/mol, which is not unrealistically high, but the reaction energy for the tetrahedral intermediate is 25.2 kcal/mol relative to the homoserine lactone (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The reaction energy for the tetrahedral intermediate is 25.2 kcal/mol relative to homoserine lactone.
source: The calculated barrier for this step is 17.5 kcal/mol, which is not unrealistically high, but the reaction energy for the tetrahedral intermediate is 25.2 kcal/mol relative to the homoserine lactone (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: DFT calculations indicate that Svi3-3 forms homoserine lactone, but that further breakdown to homoserine does not occur in the active site.
source: Thus, the DFT calculations indicate that Svi3-3 forms homoserine lactone, but that further breakdown to homoserine does not occur in the active site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the high energy barrier for tetrahedral intermediate formation.

claim: The carboxyl group of SAM is essential for the degradation of SAM by Svi3-3.
source: One prediction from the suggested reaction mechanism is that the carboxyl group of SAM is essential for the degradation of SAM by Svi3-3.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a prediction from the DFT mechanism.

claim: No Svi3-3-catalyzed production of MTA from dcSAM was observed.
source: In support of the proposed mechanism, we observed no Svi3-3-catalyzed production of MTA from dcSAM (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8.

claim: dcSAM does not induce thermal stabilization of Svi3-3.
source: However, in a DSF binding assay, dcSAM does not induce a thermal stabilization of Svi3-3 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The carboxyl group of SAM is required for binding to Svi3-3.
source: Comparison with the strong stabilization by SAM/MTA and SAH (Figure 4B) suggests that the carboxyl group of SAM is required for binding to Svi3-3.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on DSF data.

claim: A reaction product with mobility and color distinct from homoserine was observed on TLC for Svi3-3.
source: Interestingly, we observed a reaction product with mobility and color upon staining distinct from homoserine, proving that Svi3-3 is not a SAM hydrolase.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing TLC experiments.

claim: For all three enzymes (Svi3-3, T3 SAMase, and Orf1), a reaction product is observed that migrates and stains similar to homoserine lactone on TLC.
source: The same assay was performed with T3 SAMase and Orf1 and comparison with reference samples shows that for all three enzymes, a reaction product is observed that on TLC migrates and stains similar to homoserine lactone (Figure 9A), supporting the hypothesis that Svi3-3, T3 SAMase and Orf1 are indeed SAM lyases.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 9A.

claim: NMR results confirm that homoserine lactone is formed on the same time scale as MTA.
source: The results confirm that homoserine lactone is formed on the same time scale as MTA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing NMR experiments.

claim: Homoserine lactone is transformed to homoserine through spontaneous hydrolysis upon incubation in phosphate buffer at pH 7.4.
source: Upon incubation of homoserine lactone in phosphate buffer at pH 7.4, the lactone is transformed to homoserine through spontaneous hydrolysis (Figure 9—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 3.

claim: There are only two previous examples of enzymes that can cleave a trialkyl sulfonium substrate.
source: There is no previously established reaction mechanism for these enzymes, and to our knowledge there are only two previous examples of enzymes that can cleave a trialkyl sulfonium substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: ACC synthase is a distinct type of SAM lyase that exists in higher plants and some fungi.
source: A distinct type of SAM lyase, 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate synthase (ACC synthase, EC 4.4.1.14) exists in higher plants and some fungi.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: ACC synthase produces MTA and 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate.
source: The products of this enzyme are MTA and 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate that is used in the biosynthetic pathway for ethylene.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: ACC synthase is PLP-dependent and structurally and mechanistically unrelated to phage-encoded SAM lyases.
source: The reaction is PLP-dependent and the enzyme is structurally and mechanistically unrelated to the phage encoded SAM lyases (Capitani et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Capitani et al., 1999.

claim: Svi3-3 shows structural similarity to PII and PII-like proteins.
source: Instead, Svi3-3 shows structural similarity to PII and PII-like proteins, many of which bind nucleotides or nucleotide-derived metabolites in the inter-subunit clefts.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: PII and PII-like proteins have been suggested to have arisen by divergent evolution from a common ancestor.
source: Despite very low levels of sequence identity within those families, they have been suggested to have arisen by divergent evolution from a common ancestor (Forchhammer and Lüddecke, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Forchhammer and Lüddecke, 2016.

claim: No interaction was detected between Svi3-3 and ATP, ADP, or AMP by DSF.
source: Based on this similarity, we tested binding of ATP, ADP, and AMP to Svi3-3 by DSF, but detected no interaction.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Svi3-3 and PII/PII-like proteins may have a distant evolutionary relationship.
source: Still, these two families of enzymes may have a distant evolutionary relationship.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation based on structural similarity.

claim: Svi3-3 forms a trimer in solution both in the absence and in the presence of substrate.
source: Svi3-3 forms a trimer in solution both in the absence and in the presence of substrate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Stabilization of Svi3-3 by ligand binding is caused by tightening of the trimer around the ligand.
source: Comparisons of the apo and ligand-bound structures (Figure 3) as well as MD simulations (Figure 6B) indicate that stabilization is caused by tightening of the trimer around the ligand.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on structural comparisons and MD data.

claim: Binding of SAM may be associated with conformational changes that are incompatible with crystal packing or crystallization conditions for the E69Q mutant.
source: Results presented here show that E69 in Svi3-3 plays a critical role in the enzyme, and the failure in getting crystals of an E69Q mutant with SAM suggests that binding of SAM may be associated with conformational changes that are incompatible with crystal packing or with the crystallization conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation based on failed crystallization attempts.

claim: The complex structure of wild-type Svi3-3 with SAH may not fully mimic the substrate-bound state.
source: The observation that the E69Q mutant binds SAM but does not bind SAH indicates that although SAH only lacks one methyl group compared to SAM, the complex structure of WT Svi3-3 with SAH may not fully mimic the substrate-bound state.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on differential binding of SAM and SAH by the E69Q mutant.

claim: Any difference in binding mode between SAM and SAH is likely to involve the methionine end of the substrate.
source: Since MTA and SAH show a perfect overlap between the two structures (Figure 2D), any such difference in binding mode between SAM and SAH is likely to involve the methionine end of the substrate, where MD indicates that Tyr58 forms a cation-π interaction with the positively charged sulfur.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on structural analysis and MD simulations.

claim: The E69Q mutant does not bind SAH because Q69 cannot accept two hydrogen bonds and there is no positive charge on the sulfur for cation-π interaction.
source: The reason why the E69Q mutant does not bind to SAH may be that two important interactions are lacking; Q69 cannot accept two hydrogen bonds (Figure 2C) and there is no positive charge on the sulfur that can participate in the cation-π interaction with Tyr58 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an explanation for differential binding.

claim: TLC and NMR show unambiguously that Svi3-3 is a SAM lyase forming homoserine lactone and MTA.
source: Prompted by DFT calculations producing high energy barriers for a hydrolysis reaction within the active site of Svi3-3 (Figure 7B), the TLC assays and NMR show unambiguously that Svi3-3 is a SAM lyase forming homoserine lactone and MTA (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 9.

claim: Homoserine lactone is spontaneously converted to homoserine in solution.
source: The lactone is spontaneously converted to homoserine in solution (Wu et al., 1983; Figure 9—figure supplement 3, Figure 10).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Wu et al., 1983 and shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 3.

claim: Previous attempts to set up a coupled SAM hydrolase activity assay for Svi3-3 using homoserine dehydrogenase or homoserine kinase failed to show homoserine production at the same rate as MTA production.
source: Previous attempts to set up a coupled SAM hydrolase activity assay for Svi3-3 using homoserine dehydrogenase or homoserine kinase failed to show homoserine production with the same rate as MTA production (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The observed rates in coupled assays were 1000-fold lower than MTA production due to slow un-catalyzed formation of homoserine from homoserine lactone.
source: The observed rates were 1000-fold lower, and we can now explain that this is due to the slow and un-catalyzed formation of homoserine from the homoserine lactone that is enzymatically formed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section explaining previous failed assays.

claim: Non-enzymatic degradation of SAM to homoserine lactone and MTA is slowed down by favorable interactions of the carboxylate group with water.
source: Computational work by others suggests that the non-enzymatic degradation of SAM to homoserine lactone and MTA is slowed down by the favorable interactions of the carboxylate group with water (Lankau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Lankau et al., 2017.

claim: Svi3-3 increases the reactivity of the carboxylate group by excluding water from the corresponding part of the active site.
source: Thus, Svi3-3 increases the reactivity of the carboxylate group by excluding water from the corresponding part of the active site, while stabilizing a reactive conformation of the substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an explanation for catalysis.

claim: For the unimolecular reaction mechanism, only very few strictly conserved residues are required.
source: For this unimolecular reaction mechanism (Figure 10A), only very few strictly conserved residues are required, as illustrated in the multiple-sequence alignment (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both hydrogen bond acceptors of Glu69 seem critical for stabilization of the reactive state.
source: Both hydrogen bond acceptors of Glu69 seem critical for stabilization of the reactive state (Figure 10), and Svi3-3 E69Q has nearly abolished activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 10.

claim: The effect of the E68Q mutation in T3 SAMase is not as dramatic as in Svi3-3.
source: However, the effect of the corresponding mutation in T3 SAMase is not quite as dramatic.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section comparing mutational effects.

claim: Additional interactions may contribute to stabilizing the reactive state in T3 SAMase.
source: Since the level of sequence identity between the two enzymes is low, there will be many differences in the active site, and additional interactions may contribute to stabilizing the reactive state for the same mechanism in T3 SAMase.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation about T3 SAMase mechanism.

claim: T3 SAMase has no structural similarity to the OCR protein.
source: The first structure from the SAM lyase enzyme family that we present here clearly proves that they have no structural similarity to the OCR protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: T3 SAMase is a lyase and not a hydrolase.
source: Instead, our data shows that also the T3 SAMase is a lyase and not a hydrolase, but future studies are needed to elucidate whether these enzymes also have additional mechanisms of anti-restriction activity (Spoerel et al., 1979).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The same enzymatic activity as T3 SAMase was found in extract from bacteria and yeast.
source: Around the same time as the SAM-degrading enzyme from bacteriophage T3 was discovered, the same enzymatic activity was also found in extract from bacteria (Shapiro and Mather, 1958) and yeast (Mudd, 1959a; Mudd, 1959b).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Shapiro and Mather, 1958 and Mudd, 1959a; Mudd, 1959b.

claim: In bacterial and yeast systems, the reaction products were described as MTA and γ-aminobutyro-lactone (homoserine lactone).
source: In both of these systems, the reaction products were described as MTA and γ-aminobutyro-lactone (homoserine lactone), and the conversion to homoserine was considered to be spontaneous.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The phage enzyme from T3 was described as a SAM hydrolase and referred to as such until this study.
source: In contrast, the phage enzyme from T3 was early described as a SAM hydrolase, and referred to as such until this day.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: In early literature, homoserine lactone was identified as an intermediate in T3 SAMase reaction.
source: In the early literature, homoserine lactone was identified as an intermediate (Gold et al., 1964) but, perhaps due to the available methods at the time, it was not realized that homoserine was formed on a different time-scale from MTA, indicating a spontaneous and not enzyme-catalyzed reaction.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Gold et al., 1964.

claim: The functional annotation of T3 SAMase can now be corrected to SAM lyase.
source: For this reason, it is not until now that we can correct the functional annotation to SAM lyase.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as the main conclusion.

claim: SAM lyases show very low sequence conservation and large variations in size.
source: The SAM lyases show very low sequence conservation and large variations in size (Figure 5), and future studies will elucidate the relationship between structure and activity in this family of enzymes, their prevalence, and their exact biological roles in different organisms.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 5.
